intimate

/IN-tuh-mayt/ — this verb ends like 'mate': say 'IN-tuh-MAYT' · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To intimate is to make something known indirectly.

Rather than name the winner early, the judge merely intimated that the results would surprise everyone.

Worked Example

During the awards banquet, the principal never said who had won the scholarship. But she caught Lena's eye, smiled, and mentioned that 'someone in the front row' should prepare a speech — and Lena was sitting front and center.

The principal intimated the result — she made it known through hints rather than direct statement. To 'announce' is to state something openly; to intimate is to let the meaning slip through indirectly.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

imply: To imply is to suggest something without stating it directly — the meaning rides inside what you do say. To intimate is the same indirect act with a quieter, more deliberate touch: the speaker plants the meaning in tone, timing, or a look. Every intimation implies something; intimate stresses how softly it is done.

hint: To hint is to point toward something indirectly, and hints can be broad, playful, even loud — a child hints hard about a birthday gift. To intimate is subtler and more controlled: the meaning sits just beneath the surface, where only an alert listener will catch it.

allude: To allude is to refer to something without naming it — a passing nod to a thing the audience already knows, the way a speech might allude to a famous defeat. To intimate is to convey new information indirectly. You allude to what is already known; you intimate what has not yet been said.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

declare: to state openly and plainly

announce: to make known publicly

Where it sits · how deeply the hint is buried — suggest → intimate → insinuate

suggest vs. intimate: Suggest is weaker than intimate — a suggestion is offered openly and casually, while to intimate is to plant meaning deliberately beneath the surface.

insinuate vs. intimate: Insinuate is stronger than intimate — it hints slyly at something negative, adding an edge of accusation that a simple intimation lacks.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — intim-

root — intim-: inmost, innermost (Latin)

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: to make (verb-forming) (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin intimare meant 'to make known what is inmost.' To intimate is to bring an inner thought only partway to the surface — making it known by hint rather than open statement.

Use the root in a new word: intimation

Use the root in a new word: intimation: The only intimation of trouble was a brief flicker of the lights before the blackout.
